lessons.title: Ways to collect farm data
lessons.html:
What is farm data?

Data is information we write down or measure. On a farm, data tells the farmer what is happening and helps him or her make good decisions. Examples:

  • litres of milk from each cow,
  • number of eggs from each house,
  • rainfall each day,
  • mass of calves at weaning,
  • number of animals in each camp,
  • crates of fruit picked in each block,
  • feed, fuel and sprays used.

Simple ways to collect data

MethodExample
CountingCounting sheep through a gate, eggs in trays, dead birds in a house
MeasuringRain in the rain gauge, temperature on a thermometer, mass on a scale
ObservingSeeing which cow is lame, which plants have pests, what the weather is like
AskingAsking the tractor driver how many hours he worked

Writing it down

Data is only useful if it is written down correctly. Use the form, book or phone app the farm gives you. Every record needs:

  • the date (and time if needed),
  • where: camp, pen, house or block,
  • what was counted or measured,
  • the number and unit, for example 25 mm, 12 kg, 340 eggs,
  • your name.

Write clearly. A 1 that looks like a 7 can cause a big mistake. If you make a mistake, cross it out with one line and write the right number next to it. Do not rub out or guess.

A farm example

Every morning at 08:00, Nomsa reads the rain gauge next to the farm office. She writes the date, 12 mm and her name in the rain book, then empties the gauge. At the end of the month the farmer adds up the rainfall to plan planting.

lessons.title: Collecting, reporting and caring for equipment
lessons.html:
Follow the method you are given

Your supervisor will tell you what to collect, how, and when. Do it the same way every time. For example, read the rain gauge at the same time every morning, or weigh calves on the same scale. If you change the method, the numbers cannot be compared.

Reporting

  • Hand in your forms or send your records at the time agreed, usually every day or week.
  • Tell your supervisor straight away about anything unusual: very low milk, many dead chickens, a sudden pest outbreak, or a broken water pipe.
  • If you could not collect data, say so. Never make up numbers.

Using and caring for equipment

EquipmentCare
Rain gaugeKeep it level and clear of grass and trees; empty after reading
ScaleCheck it shows zero before weighing; keep it clean and dry
ThermometerKeep out of direct sun unless told otherwise; handle gently
Measuring tapeWipe clean, roll up, keep dry
Phone or tabletKeep charged, in a cover, away from water and dust

Report broken or faulty equipment. A scale that reads wrong gives wrong data every time.

Health and safety

  • When weighing or counting animals, stand in a safe place and do not get between animals and a wall.
  • Wear gloves and wash your hands after handling animals, dead birds or manure.
  • In fields that were sprayed, obey the re-entry signs before going in to scout.
  • Wear a hat and drink water when working in the sun.
  • Watch for snakes when checking traps or gauges in long grass.

Key points

  • Data can be collected by counting, measuring, observing and asking.
  • Every record needs date, place, what, number and unit, and your name.
  • Use the same method every time and never make up numbers.
  • Look after equipment and report faults.
  • Work safely around animals, chemicals and in the veld.

quiz.question: Reading the rain gauge is an example of which data collection method?

options.text: The date, place, what was measured, the number with its unit and your name

quiz.question: You wrote a wrong number on the form. What should you do?

options.text: Rub it out until it is gone
Cross it out with one line and write the right number next to it

Why should you use the same method every time?

options.text: So the numbers can be compared
